title: Prepare, use, act, benefit, and learn
author: David Shannon
source: More tips on how to use this book.doc, circulated 6 September 2016. Earlier draft wording ('100 Power Questions' and 'XX' situations) retained; the published collection contains 99 questions. The source's comparison table is set out as text.
paragraphs: The Worshipful Company of Management Consultants, one of the City of London's respected Livery Companies is proud to offer this volume to the widest possible audience in the assurance that the authors have produced an outstanding aid to better management. We urge you to ask, and answer, these questions.
The heart of the book is the collection of 100 Power Questions. We here suggest a five step approach to using these questions to best effect.
These questions may be used in any of three main modes:

By asking oneself the questions; by arranging for someone else with whom you have a working relationship to ask you the questions; or by someone independent of your management asking you the questions.
Self questioning. Advantages: fast, private, and secure. Disadvantages: lack of challenge, only one point of view. A good place to start.
Related questioning. Advantages: challenge, a second point of view. Disadvantages: slower, interested second party. Probable first further option used.

Independent questioning. Advantages: challenge, added perspective, and discipline. Disadvantages: slower to arrange, identifying a good questioner, cost, and false starts. Likely to be the most powerful approach.

Asking and answering these questions requires a desire to improve performance, an open mind and honest answering. By open mind we mean clearly listening to the question in full and understanding it before considering and formulating your personal answer. To this end on the question pages we give hints as to the issues worth considering in the context of particular questions.

Users should also recognise that entering on this questioning is like starting a journey with no fixed end in sight. Like any learning it should be an adventure. We hope you will find valuable new insights affecting your decisions and behaviour.
Your concept of value is likely to be something along the following lines:

'To realise improvements in my management practices that translate into measurable achievement of benefits to myself, to the organisations for whom I work and for the wider society, with minimum cost to myself and others.'

The price of obtaining these questions is the least of your costs and should pale into insignificance in relation to the benefits obtained. The most major resource use is likely to be your commitment, in time, thought and personal emotion. The best approach to maximising value is enthusiastically to pursue the benefits.

These Power Questions may be asked of a group, however we feel it important that members of such a group first have some experience of using the questions personally and also that the whole group consents to their use.

Finally, in preparation you should appreciate the way these questions are presented. The types of questions vary between short and long, between direct, probing and open questions. However, the three categories used for presentation are of a different order, these are:
Situations There are well-recognised management situations when the right question helps to illuminate appropriate action. We identify XX of these and link them to particular relevant questions.
Dimensions All questions have been identified as belonging to one or more of the Ten Dimensions. These dimensions, indexed and explained above, cover the range of concerns of every manager.
Trees Many questions are linked together as if the roots and branches of trees. Thus there are suggested sequences of questions that either probe underlying issues or work through consequences.
In addition, we provide a full index of key words to be found in questions. This can be used to select suitable questions related to your particular concern.
Use

Power Question should be used one at a time. So, where to start? There is no rule, the options include: using Situations, Dimensions, or the Index or even random selection as an initial screen. Once started the suggested Links may be found useful.

The three stages of asking the question, considering and exploring the question, and then answering should be clearly separated. These are not facile questions, so time spent fully appreciating the question before answering will not be wasted. A fourth stage of assessing the validity of the answer may often prove beneficial, possibly leading to a modified or substantially different answer.

For all questions we have included a brief description of the likely insights. This is to help you develop a response that leads to action where warranted. Responses might include the belief that this question is not applicable or not illuminating for you now, recognition that your current performance on the issue is valid and needs no change or acknowledgement that a change in your practice would be beneficial. Such a change might require new knowledge, changed communications such as self-disclosure or questioning or obtaining further input to explore the accuracy and significance of your answer.
Here are some final tips on using the questions:
Use these questions in your most productive time
Do not duck difficult questions
Skip a question that does not resonate with you now
Only ask questions within your attention span, not too many in one session
Revisit one question as often as you wish
Consider whether your answer is different when relaxed, in a typical situation or when under stress
Note your answers
Note your response
Add actions to your response note.
The question pages have been set out to help with this process.
Act

Your responses should have provided potential actions. Commit to those you think most likely to yield benefits and integrate these actions into your general action list. Do not add more actions if you already have sufficient for your time and energy available. As with any action list review frequently, preferably to a schedule, and record progress.
Do include actions which benefit other users of these questions thus implementing one of our Company's mottos, 'giving and gaining'.
Benefit
The purpose of assembling these questions and of presenting them here is so that you and others benefit from their use. Two types of benefit are possible:
1. Direct management benefit to you and your organization from your increased effectiveness.
2. Improvement and extended use of these questions by others, through personal recommendation or by providing feedback to the authors.
We strongly recommend obtaining feedback from others when identifying benefits.
Learning
Through reflection on your questioning process you should improve your capacity to use these questions.
If you have prepared yourself by reading this section, have decided on an initial mode of questioning and on an appropriate technique, you are ready to address your first question.

title: The incisive questions technique
author: Author not recorded
source: The Incisive Questions technique.docx, circulated for the website, 6 September 2016. No byline is recorded on the recovered attachment.
paragraphs: The Incisive Questions technique. Incisive questions are the tools of all great leaders.
Most of our 99 Questions can be further extended using a technique to turn them into incisive questions.
First, strip out limiting assumptions from your answers! Take a look at our question No. 16. 'How do I ensure the welfare of my team?'
To which your initial answer might be: 'There's not much I can do, because the important controls are managed by Human Resources.'

Tackling that limiting assumption, the reformulated incisive question might then read, 'If I controlled the influence of Human Resources, how would I ensure the welfare of my team?' This now frees you to explore the options, and to encourage participation in effective action.
Second, having answered the Question, then reformulate the Question in the light of your answer so as to replace the limiting assumption with a liberating one.

For example, you want to talk to your boss, but feel you can't do it. Ask yourself, 'What might you be assuming that is stopping you?' You reply, 'I'm afraid he'll simply laugh at me and think I'm stupid.' After more thought, you realise that you too are assuming that you are stupid. The assumption sits there, holding you back, limiting your thinking.

A colleague might say, 'So what if he laughs? You're not stupid; go and talk to him!' You say, 'OK', but still you put it off... just telling you to do it won't work. But a question will, because, unlike a statement which requires you to obey, a Question requires you to think.
Third having rephrased the Question to replace the limiting assumption, form your next question by replacing your limiting with an appropriate liberating one.
The key to forming this next question is listening with precision in order to reformulate the question.
'If you knew that you were intelligent [the liberating assumption], how would you talk to your boss?'
Incisive questions that have made a difference to people's lives and organisations:
'If you were not to hold back in your life, what would you be doing?'
'If you knew you were vital to this organisation's success, how would you approach your work?'
'If you were to become chief executive, what problem would you solve first, and how would you do it?'
'If things could be exactly right for you in this situation, how would they have had to change?'
'If you knew something wonderful was going to happen today, how would you feel?'
Note that the first part of each question asserts a positive assumption; the second part directs the thinker's attention back to their issue or goal.
And when you get stuck?
Use incisive questioning to identify your own assumptions and create your own questions to remove them.

Ask yourself, 'What am I assuming here that is stopping me?' Listen to the answer, which might be, 'I am assuming that I don't deserve success here'. Then strip out that assumption and form a new question 'If I knew that I do deserve success here, what would I do right now?'

If you want to feel better, ask yourself, 'What am I assuming that is making me feel depressed?' Note the answer, 'I am assuming that I have no choice here – that I am powerless.' And then remove it, 'If I knew that I do have a choice here and am powerful in this situation, how would I feel?'

If your team has run out of good ideas, ask yourselves, 'What might we be assuming here that is limiting our thinking on this issue?' Remember the answer, which could be, 'We are assuming that only the top people can think about this adequately.' Then remove it, 'If we knew that we can think about this as well as anybody, what would our ideas be now?'

title: My first 100 days
author: David Glassman
source: David Glassman Blog contribution.docx, circulated for the website, 6 September 2016.
paragraphs: Before I started coaching as a professional I had proper jobs. In one new role, I tried the coaching approach that had been successful elsewhere and I asked questions. The top team members provided answers, but I soon got the sense that they were the ones they thought I wanted to hear rather than the 'right' ones. The conversations soon began to seem like inquisitions, both to me and to them, and it became a challenge not to 'tell' instead of to 'ask'.

On reflection, I realised that change would depend upon my behaviour. My questions were not generating the responses I needed not because the answers were wrong, but because I was asking the wrong questions.

I had to be clear about my goals, ensure they were congruent with the organisation's aims, and communicated in a way that recognised the perceptions of the team, individually and collectively. Soon, they knew what I would ask and tailored their efforts and priorities to those questions, cascading the approach down through the organisation. With everyone feeling a co-author, success was shared and enjoyed by all.

title: Taking feedback seriously
author: David Shannon
source: SituationApplDS01-2.doc, circulated for the website, 6 September 2016.
paragraphs: A book keeper in the client's administration queried the fee request record of one of my consulting team. She had spotted that the team member's attendance record differed from the claim account. It transpired that the team member had agreed with his client supervising manager to work overtime on a few days so that he could leave early one weekend.
This fits the book's Situation 4 'An external party raises doubts about the ability of a key member of my team.'

Looking through the questions associated with this Situation I come across Question 36 'What do I do to demonstrate that I take feedback seriously.' I should have considered this question because 'If I don't demonstrate that I take feedback seriously, I am indicating that I am not open to feedback in the future.' If only I had considered this Question 36 carefully at the time.
To what extent I value the views of those with whom I work.
Am I truly a team player?
Am I avoiding giving and requesting feedback? If so, why might that be?
Most importantly I would have realized that administrative members of the client's organization were also necessary members of the assignment team.

As it was, although the immediate issue was resolved, the administrator was, I fear, left with a feeling that we had not taken her feedback seriously enough. In the light of using this question and associated insights I would have done much more to embrace the feedback and make the administrator feel part of the team.
Was it just coincidence that shortly afterwards we failed to secure further work with this, at the time, our most important client?

title: Working through a situation: a profit warning
author: Gia Campari
source: Working through a situation.docx, circulated 27 September 2016. A few question quotations use the companion draft's wording.
paragraphs: You've found a situation in the book that reflects where you are at the moment: Situation 16. 'I have to issue a profit warning', so you start browsing through the suggested questions.

The suggested questions are listed in numerical order, not in order of importance. Each person will be surprised by a different question. Each person will have different answers because each person's situation will be different. Not all the questions are relevant to everybody, that is why a selection is offered.
4. What would I rather others did not know?

What's behind the profit warning? Have I been protecting someone and do not wish others to know? Did someone try to warn me and I did not believe it? (How many CEOs surround themselves with 'yes-men'!). We all have something we would rather others did not know and in some cases this may have a very negative impact on the organisation.

This question points you to questions: 54. 'What is my worst nightmare?' - this may be relevant! I'll definitely look at it later; 82. 'What Am I pretending not to know or see?' - this may be similar to the question I am already considering, so will put it aside for the moment, and 83. 'What decision am I avoiding?' - Hmm, this makes me think, I'd better take a look at it.
9. How adaptable is my organisation?

A supremely important question in this situation! A profit warning could be the result of decreased sales/margins or cost spiralling out of control. More often than not it is a question of sales/margins. If our profits are below last year's quarter, what changes in our market have we not adapted to? Are we too rigid in our approach? Have we been repeating what made us successful in the past? (nothing fails like success!) Understanding how flexible we are is fundamental to understanding the cause of the profit warning. What have we failed to do? What have we failed to adapt to? What can we learn from that? Answer to these questions may well help us structure an intelligent communication to our stakeholders, who should be more reassured if we tell them what we have learned from the profit warning than by hearing a cock & bull story.

This question points you to questions: 8. 'What are the current constraints on growth?' - this may be worth exploring - is the profit warning a result of a too rapid expansion? Or lack of growth? ; 55. 'How do I survive and flourish

faster than my environment?' I wasn't expecting this one and it's made me think of how I can make the best of the situation; 86. What's getting in the way of me getting things done and reaching my and the organisation's potential?' - something to discuss with my team?
11. Who are my five key stakeholders?

Who are they? How well do we know them? Am I only considering the obvious? What are their concerns? How will each group take the profit warning? I need to answer to them all and communicate differently to them all.

This question points you to questions: 14. 'Who is really my boss?' Who do I have to answer to? How will they take this? things to think about; 81. what attracts customers and employees to my organisation?' this helps me focus on the positive, as customers are still attracted - it also makes me think of what we may have done to lose customers; 98. 'How do I learn about my customer's needs?' in the same category of the previous question; I must know my customers if I aspire to their loyalty.
17. How can I ensure that everyone understands the profit and loss statement?

Looking at the cost side of the income-expenditure equation, how many people really understand our business model - how we make money? How we make money means how we make a profit, not how we sell. If everyone understood this, we'd have early signals of anything going amiss. We may even have avoided the need to issue a profit warning. A most pertinent question.

This question points you to questions: 10. 'What proportion of my staff can explain our business model?' This makes me think that everyone is focused on their individual targets and collectively we may have lost sight of the whole ; 18. 'What is the first thing I could do to improve cashflow?' This seems the most obvious question and one that gets us immediately into action. Nothing like a crisis to focus the organisation. ; 43. How much time do I allow my people for training and personal development?' It may be too late now, but think about how this may have impacted the outcome you are dealing with. If none, maybe I'd do things differently next time. If plenty, then time to rethink the training strategy.
By the end of all this pondering, you may well be able to view your situation in a different light and take actions that may not have occurred to you before your reflections.

title: The source of her ruse
author: David Shannon
source: Limerick David Shannon.docx, circulated for the website, 6 September 2016. One typographical error corrected.
paragraphs:
There was a young girl from The City
Whose wealth grew with alacrity
The source of her ruse
Was not the A's but the Q's
That enriched her perspicacity

title: Into the unknown
author: David Shannon
source: BlogDS260117.docx, circulated 26 January 2017. Written during the Brexit debate; references to political office and future events belong to that date. The original email response invitation has been omitted.
paragraphs: So, we in the UK are venturing again into the unknown darkness reaching out our hand in the dark - and the fist we seem today to be grasping is that of Donald Trump divisive President elect of USA. How will the arguments over Brexit develop, whether hard or soft, whether secret or disclosed, whether conducted bilaterally or multi-laterally? Many are afraid of the complexity and of the implications. BUT, what if this is the wrong question?

Question framing is one of the most powerful tools in a leader's kit, whether managing a small enterprise, a Division, a Company or a Country. We authors of The 99 Essential Business Questions compiled this guide to powerful questioning. Applying our framework to the Brexit debate and looking through our book for a Situation close to that facing our Prime Minister we find the Situation 7:
A crisis arises which could destroy my team.
This may well resonate with the occupant of No. 10 Downing Street. Following the links from this Situation to the five selected questions from the 99 we find Question No. 9:
How adaptable is my organisation?
The adjacent commentary provides four short paragraphs on why to ask oneself this question and four short paragraphs on the insights expected. To take just one each of these:
Why ask? Anticipating barriers will help to surmount them.
Insight? To identify the energy sappers.

Thinking creatively through such provocations May might come up with the view that focusing on Brexit is both a barrier and an energy sapper. As a result of our referendum the UK is not after all engaged just in Brexit. Such an exit concentrates the forces against change and focus diverts energy from other vital work. There is another answer inspired by the adaptability question: that we have to address not just one project but one Project and a separate Programme.

The Brexit Project, readily defined in terms of initiation, stakeholders, phases, protocols, timescale and end-state is to exit the EU. In just over two years UK's membership of the EU will be in the past.

The future orientated Programme is to redefine UK relations with all other countries and blocks. Whilst this has some links with Brexit it nevertheless consists of several projects starting over a long period, includes non-project elements, lasts much longer, has much less clearly defined success criteria, has a more flexible budget and has success criteria still being developed. A subsidiary question now becomes what to call the Programme so as to focus people's minds on this positive work instead of merely on the negative exit effort. Suggestions to date include:
1. BRenter 2. BRelease 3. BRUKFree 4. FreeUK 5. NewUK

This example of the use of our book may be at a higher level than your current business opportunity, but working through such challenging questions may bring you and your team also valuable insights towards engaging more positively with your future and greater success.
We all venture into unknown futures, but the right questions can direct us to reach out in the right direction.

title: Introduction to dimensions
author: David Shannon
source: Introduction to DimensionsDSB.doc, circulated 29 May 2015. Describes the earlier ten-dimension framework, removed before publication.
paragraphs: Our team identified ninety-nine powerful questions for directors and managers. Considering these it became clear that the questions addressed a number of major issues affecting organizations and the people in them. Identification and analysis of these issues led to defining ten distinct types of organizational and personal concerns. These we labelled Dimensions.

Each Dimension was refined to a distinct definition. These definitions include a title using terms for the two extremes of its continuous range, thus for example the first Dimension concerns the organizational issue of management focus and performance. It is labelled Process – Outcomes.

For each Dimension we provide a pithy saying to highlight its focus, usually illustrated by a cartoon. We explain why the Dimension is important, and then provide a textual explanation of the Dimension. A 'real world' example from our collective experience is also provided together with a short bullet-point summary.

We are familiar with the several existing diagnostic frameworks for organizations and teams. However this entirely new tool derives directly from our body of questions. As well as adding great value to our book, we believe that these Dimensions form a comprehensive framework for diagnosing organisational issues. As aids for understanding and communication they are widely useful management concepts.

title: Family or work or both?
author: Gia Campari
source: Family or work or both?.docx, prepared for Family Friendly Working, 13 October 2016. Original 2016 text.
paragraphs: At some stage of our lives, we all have to choose how much time we dedicate to work and how much to children, partner, family, friends or simply to ourselves. Numerous studies have shown that efficiency at work increases if we take breaks and have outside interests. New ideas and new ways of solving problems, so important in today's conceptual economy, often come to us when we allow the problem to 'gestate', (in the words of Poincaré), while doing something completely different. It would make sense therefore, for employers - including ourselves if we are self employed - to require us to take breaks and spend time away from work!

That rarely happens so we need to take the matter into our own hands and find a solution that is best suited to our situation. Perhaps a few tips on what has worked for others and what questions we could be asking ourselves, may help us find that solution.

A few tips: 1. Schedule activities and block out time in your diary to spend with children, family, etc. and treat it as you would a meeting with your most important client or shareholder – cancelling is not an option! 2. Learn to say 'No' without feeling guilty. Take a course, read a book on the subject, ask someone who is already good at it. 3. If you have to work late, take the work home instead and finish it after dinner when the children are asleep and your partner is watching TV. This ensures you have a family dinner and you can catch up on what has been happening in your family members' lives that day. 4. Pass your knowledge onto colleagues who could step in for you in an emergency. It should be common practice in organisations, but we know that common practice is often uncommon. 5. Learn to delegate – a notorious weakness of many people, not only managers! 6. Ask for help. We instinctively want to help, but are much more reluctant to ask for help. 7. Find a mentor who has succeeded in taking time for him or herself and ask for advice.
Questions you could be asking yourself to uncover the root of the problem:

1. Am I a workaholic or do I just love my job? In either case, am I willing to sacrifice my relationships with my children, partners or friends? 2. What do I really want from my relationships? Both at work and outside work? How much time am I willing to dedicate to them? Which are most important for me? 3. How do I measure success? Is it in terms of my authority at work, my social status or the quality of my relationships? 4. What would I like my legacy to be? Am I an influencer at work? How would I like to influence people who look up to me? How would I like my children to approach their work? 5. Could I use a mentor or a coach? Do I look after myself as well as I look after others? Could I use some help or advice?

6. Are my priorities consistent with my purpose in life? Do I know what my purpose in life is? Should I spend some time clarifying it? It would help me take the right decisions for me. 7. What decision am I avoiding? Deep down, do I know what I have to do, but do not want to face up to it?
Finally, make sure that you believe that you will find the right solution for you and you will!

title: Why I would hire David Brent — and why I wouldn't
author: Gia Campari
source: Why I would hire:not hire David Brent.docx, prepared for a Real Business magazine request, 18 August 2016.
paragraphs: why I would hire him

1. He would do all my dirty work for me, no matter how embarrassing as he would not realise it's embarrassing! 2. He would promote teamwork - people would find something that unites them all: laughing/rolling their eyes behind his back! 3. He makes everyone look good - both in terms of competence and dress sense - so people would feel motivated to do their best to show him up even more. 4. Employees would be happier - to know they will not be going home to someone like him! Happy people are more creative and productive.
Why I would not hire him

1. Zero relationship skills - the most important skill to have as a manager is to be able to build relationships based on trust with your colleagues. He does not have a clue on how to go about it. 2. He seems to be blissfully unaware of the impact that his words and actions have on other people, so is incapable of influencing them. 3. He does not seem to care about other people. 4. He looks after only No.1 - himself 5. He is incapable of getting the best out of people.

title: How can I use this book?
author: The authors
source: possible article how can I use this book?.docx, circulated 2 July 2016. Original draft wording and examples; situation references belong to that version.
paragraphs: How can I use this book? Dip into it when you are stuck with a problem or need to resolve a situation, initiate a dialogue with others, stimulate ideas or find a route to an answer. Open it at random, browse through the Questions – where do they lead you? You could more logically start by identifying the Situation you find yourself in. Is it something External, over which you have no control? Is it Internal – something arising from inside? Does it involve a Team of people? Or is it something Personal? The Book at A Glance diagram on page 27 will help you find either your exact situation or something that approximates to it and from which you can work. Having found your situation, try the suggested questions. Are there further questions those questions suggest? Your answers to these questions should lead to action. If so, you now know how to use the book, the purpose of which is to impact people like yourself in management! Suppose you have just lost a major order that both you and your boss were certain you would win. If you were well educated you would ask your client why you were not chosen. Then you would probably try and construct a Fishbone Diagram to examine the causes and their effects that led to the failure to secure the order. However, the Fishbone Diagram can only contain things you already know it cannot give a new perspective on the problem. You might even try a 'Mystery Shopper' to find out the client's experience with your organisation. However, the Mystery Shopper can never replicate the exact conditions in which your lost client was considering your offer. This book does not advocate abandoning such well-tried methods as Fishbone Diagrams and Mystery Shoppers to gain insight into your situations. But this book does offer precisely some further insightful questions which will help. So what would you have said silently to yourself after doing your Fishbone Diagram and listening to your Mystery Shopper's report? a. What an idiot! How could I have let that happen? b. Am I going to keep my job? c. What can I learn from this? Clearly, how you feel and what action you take will differ in each case because you are asking yourself a different question:

a. You beat yourself up; you think of everything that went wrong; you imagine how you could have said something brilliant but did not and by the end of this analysis your self-esteem has hit rock bottom. b. Your main emotion here is fear – which can be a trigger for action, but not necessarily an empowering one. More likely a very defensive one. You will make a list of all the impossible customer requirements; you will persuade yourself that the competition was willing to make this bid loss-making in order to capture the customer. You will find all the possible reasons or excuses for your lack of success – but not the springboard for future success. c. This, unlike the others, is an empowering question that will lead you to learn from your mistake (if any) and to take positive action, e.g. better preparation or better understanding of the customer to improve your chances in the future. So you reach for the book and begin to ask yourself the questions suggested by Situation 12, which is concerned with externally caused situations such as the loss of an order. Situation 12 suggests you ask yourself questions 9, 31, 38, 75, 81 or 94. Looking through the book you see that question 81 looks interesting and you ask yourself, 'What attracts customers and employees to my organisation'? You find that attraction is driven by emotion not by logic and research shows that it is a function of drive (as most clients are attracted to suppliers that have goals and are actively pursuing them), presence (being fully present with the client, through contact, listening and prioritising distraction-free conversations), spontaneity (predictability is death to attraction), intention (most customers are attracted to suppliers who strive to shine a light on all their actions and throw away the baggage they have accumulated over the years), leadership (most clients are attracted to suppliers with emotional intelligence) and vulnerability (all of the power, prestige, leadership ability and humour that you can muster won't get you anywhere with the client unless you are prepared to let them see you emotionally). You also notice that question 81 suggests you consider questions 15, 26 and 98. You see that question 98 looks interesting and so you ask yourself, 'How do I learn about my customers' needs?' You find that to get close to demanding clients, you really need to get inside their head and that there are five ways to do that. Stand in your client's shoes. Look beyond your core business and understand your client's full range of choices, as well as his or her ecosystem of suppliers, partners etc.--of which you may be part. This exercise will also deepen your understanding of competitors and help you better anticipate their moves. Staple yourself to a customer's order. Track key clients' experiences as they traverse

your company's pathways and note where the experience breaks down. If you can't exactly put yourself through a customer experience, try role-playing exercises at all points of your client's interaction with your company. Field diverse customer teams. One bank added members of the back-office support group to its customer team, supplementing the usual customer-facing roles. IBM sends senior teams from different disciplines into the field to meet customers and develop a deep understanding of how to serve them better. Learn together with customers. GE invited its top customers in China, along with local executives and account managers, to a seminar on leadership and innovation. Doing so not only helped GE executives better understand the mindset of Chinese counterparts; it also helped them to influence that mindset. Lean forward and anticipate. Focus on what clients will want tomorrow, as Steve Jobs and Richard Branson did so exquisitely. Try to envision different futures through tools like scenario planning and then explore how underlying market shifts may affect your client. This simple example which leads to you considering questions 81 and 98 in the book provides you with new insights into the situation, illustrates how the questions you ask yourself will invariably determine how you feel about a situation and what you will do about it.

title: Making decisions, accountability, growth, isolation, and change
author: David Glassman
source: BoQs article for Best Practice magazine 170110.docx, circulated 10 January 2017. Original article draft.
paragraphs: Most of us can identify with leadership roles in our workplaces. Fewer consider ourselves to be the leader of Me PLC, so our attention to personal development is a path less followed. I wonder why.

Authority from a formal leadership position seems to convey power that is actually illusory. Assuming a leadership role does not, in itself, change who you are, rather it reveals who you are. Your actions will confirm the perceptions that others have of you. Leaders cannot obfuscate or prevaricate while they look over the horizon to anticipate the unknown. Do they understand that ambiguity will be as revealing as clarity?

Leaders create leaders rather than followers. How do they build teams to tackle tasks to meet new circumstances if they recruit those who have demonstrated skills in areas no longer valid or viable? In the commercial sector, their stakeholders want them to make money; how do they do that with untried people and still minimise risk? The challenges are no less daunting in other sectors.

The above four questions are routine for leaders. The successful ones focus on just that: asking the most appropriate questions. The first answer is not necessarily the most helpful and, often, the route to last time's success will be destructive in deriving this time's solution. In essence, we need to judge ourselves and others by the questions we ask and not by the answers.
What do leaders want help with and what questions should they be asking? As an aid, remember MAGIC.

Making decisions: I have been promoted from a sectional silo and now I am responsible for areas I know little about so how do I know I have all the information I need? How do I know I am hearing the truth rather than what 'they' think I want to hear? Can I trust my team? How do I show I love them even if the appropriate thinking and effort generate the wrong outcome?

Accountability: Are my success criteria meaningful to the longer-term success of my venture? Who is holding me to account? How can I demonstrate to my stakeholders that we are all delivering to that goal?

Growth: one way or another we need to keep our organisations relevant and vibrant. How am I growing corporate and personal capacity ahead of need to more-than-satisfy our customers and make our staff grateful for the opportunities that offers for their personal fulfilment?
Isolation: it is lonely at the top. How am I relating to others in my sector, my specialisation, my profession and, most importantly, my family? What support would be facilitative?

Change: coping is insufficient. How can I learn to develop a liking for the only real certainty in life? And that is in the knowledge that some of my, and our, decisions will be plain wrong. What would it take to strengthen our resilience to knocks and set-backs?
Best practice should be the minimum acceptable in a well-led organisation. The outstanding leader will question everything to harness the ingredients for 'Even Better If'.
David Glassman One of The Seven, co-authors of The 99 Essential Business Questions (to take you beyond the obvious management actions) Published by Filament Publishing

title: Asking for a pay rise: Patrick McHugh
author: Patrick McHugh
source: Payrise sound bites for Helen.docx, five authors' responses prepared for a press request, 10 August 2016.
paragraphs: I think that this question is a Team Related Situation and that the closest situation to this in the book is Situation 26. I need to recruit a new team member. This situation suggests that we look at questions 8, 60, 61, 66, 74 and 81. I have looked at these questions and think that the most interesting are
Question 60. What do I want from my team?

The areas which should be mentioned in asking for a pay rise are therefore – how the applicant exhibits clarity of purpose, fits into the team and why they enjoy working together. Question 60 also suggests looking at questions 43, 72 and 99.
Question 66. Would I like to change the cast of players?

The area which should be mentioned in asking for a pay rise is therefore – how the applicant fits into the existing team and how well they are performing as a team member. Question 60 also suggests looking at questions 12, 72 and 92.
Both question 60 and 66 suggest looking at question 72.
Question 72. What do I do to encourage others to use their gifts?
The area which should be mentioned in asking for a pay rise is therefore – where the applicant has encouraged other members of the team to use their gifts.

title: Asking for a pay rise: David Peregrine-Jones
author: David Peregrine-Jones
source: Payrise sound bites for Helen.docx, five authors' responses prepared for a press request, 10 August 2016.
paragraphs: Questions that might be in a manager's mind that ought to be addressable if you are going to try and justify a pay rise.
How well did you perform against the challenges set in your last appraisal?
How attractive are you to other parts of this organisation?
What would it take for you to leave?
And what would we want to do if it was indeed a serious possibility?
Are you showing the 'top quartile' performance appropriate for further promotion or is a pay rise a compensation for no longer being promotable?
Also - how do you really stack up against your competitors and who survives if we have to reduce headcount?
Maybe also - how do you make me more successful?

title: Asking for a pay rise: David Glassman
author: David Glassman
source: Payrise sound bites for Helen.docx, five authors' responses prepared for a press request, 10 August 2016.
paragraphs: In summary as a sound bite: 'You need ….; I have ….; together we could …'
More specifically: How has the whole team performed against our commitment / the plan?
Has the individual's performance in the team been that of a finder, a minder or a grinder?
Is the individual a possible successor to my role within my timescale for my own personal advancement?

What are my freedoms for action on this matter in terms of overall money to spend and directions for its allocation; initiation of long-term personal development plans; ability to offer accelerated accountability on projects; mentoring or coaching opportunities; …? (Money is not the only reward that should be sought and development requests should be even more persuasive for a positive decision.)
Does s/he draw in and stimulate the involvement of peers and subordinates?
Do more senior members of the hierarchy listen to her/his views – and even canvass them?
Can s/he work on the bridge and in the engine room, simultaneously?
Is s/he respected and even loved when they take a lead at times when a leader is required?

title: Asking for a pay rise: Benjamin Taylor
author: Benjamin Taylor
source: Payrise sound bites for Helen.docx, five authors' responses prepared for a press request, 10 August 2016.
paragraphs: I'd say that I want to hear:

'This is how I'm adding value already - and this is the extra value I can add in future. Here's how it can add to the bottom line, and strengthen the team. I'd like to run at this level for three months and prove it, and if successful I'll be happy with that for at least two years'

title: Asking for a pay rise: Gia Campari
author: Gia Campari
source: Payrise sound bites for Helen.docx, five authors' responses prepared for a press request, 10 August 2016.
paragraphs: As a manager/director what would I like to see and hear when I am asked for a pay rise?
When you make a request - any request - you should think of what would make it easy for the person to say 'yes'. What would I have to see and hear to make it easy for me to give you a pay rise?

1. Evidence that you love your job 2. Examples of how you have helped colleagues whether they asked you or not 3. How you treat our company as your own 4. Evidence that you look for opportunities for improvement 5. How you take responsibility for your own competence development 6. How you pass on what you have learned to your colleagues 7. Your plan for future pay rises.
